title: Group Anagrams
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning existing groups versus a hash map keyed by sorted signature versus a count signature.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of strings strs, group every string with all of its anagrams, and return the groups in any order.

blocks.text: Given an array of strings strs, group every string with all of its anagrams, and return the groups in any order.

blocks.title: Analogy: Sorting Scrabble Racks Into Matching Bins
blocks.text: Like sorting a pile of Scrabble letter racks into bins, where every rack made from exactly the same letters, in any order, gets placed into the same bin together.

blocks.caption: Every string is grouped together with every other string that uses the exact same letters

blocks.content: {"headers":["Group","Members","Why"],"rows":[["Group 1","\"eat\", \"tea\", \"ate\" (all use e, a, t)","each is built from exactly one e, one a, and one t"],["Group 2","\"tan\", \"nat\" (both use a, n, t)","each is built from exactly one a, one n, and one t"],["Group 3","\"bat\" (no other word shares its letters)","no other string in the array uses exactly one b, one a, and one t"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Both empty strings use exactly the same (empty) set of letters","they belong in the same group","an empty signature is still a valid, shared signature"],["Answer","[[\"\", \"\"]]","a single group containing both empty strings"]]}

blocks.text: With only a single string and nothing to group it with, the answer is simply that one string in its own group by itself, [["a"]].
It helps to ask what single, shared property every anagram of a string has in common, and how that property can be used directly as a lookup key.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Valid Anagram already established that two strings are anagrams exactly when their letter multisets match, regardless of order, which is the exact property this problem needs to group by.

Observation 2: The brute force scans every existing group's representative signature to find a match, which reintroduces the same "compare against everything seen so far" shape that a hash map is specifically built to avoid.

Observation 3: Giving every string a canonical signature that only depends on its letter multiset, its sorted form is one natural choice, turns "does a matching group already exist" into a single hash map lookup, letting every string join its group in O(1) average time instead of scanning existing groups by hand.

Observation 4: Sorting each string to build that signature costs k log k per string; Valid Anagram's counting approach builds an equally valid, and cheaper, canonical signature directly from letter counts in O(k) time instead, confirmed by tracing "eat", "tea", and "tan" through the count based signature, where "eat" and "tea" produce the identical count of one each of a, e, and t and land in the same bucket automatically.

Recognizing that any signature shared by every anagram of a string, whether built by sorting or by counting, turns grouping into a direct hash map lookup is what removes the need to compare against every existing group by hand.

Maintain a list of groups built so far. For every string, compare it against one representative from each existing group by checking whether their sorted letters match, and either join a matching group or start a new one.

items: For every string, sort its letters to get a signature.
Scan every existing group's signature to see if it matches.
If a match is found, add the string to that group, otherwise start a brand new group.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Sorting a string's letters produces a signature that is identical for every anagram of that string, regardless of the original order of characters.
Every existing group is scanned in turn to check whether its stored signature matches the current string's signature.
A brand new group is only started once every existing group has been checked and none matched, guaranteeing every string ends up in exactly one group.

blocks.text: Every string is correctly matched to a group sharing its sorted letters, so this produces valid anagram groups.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times k log k), scanning every existing group for every string, with each sort costing k log k for a string of length k.
Space: O(n times k), for the groups and signatures stored.
Limitation: scanning every existing group by hand to find a match is unnecessary. A hash map can look up the correct group directly using the sorted signature as a key.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: comparing a new string's signature against every existing group's signature by hand repeats the same linear scan for every single string processed.

What a hash map fixes directly: using the signature itself as the map key turns "find the matching group" into a single O(1) average lookup, with no explicit scanning at all.

Can the signature itself be made cheaper: yes, sorting costs k log k per string, but a character count built in one linear pass is an equally valid canonical signature.

The core idea: use any signature shared by every anagram of a string as the hash map key directly, and prefer a counted signature over a sorted one to avoid the log factor entirely.

Use a hash map from a sorted signature to the list of strings sharing it. For every string, compute its sorted signature once, and append it directly to the map entry for that signature, creating a new entry only if needed. This replaces scanning every existing group with a single constant time average lookup per string.
A hash map keyed by each string's sorted signature.

blocks.caption: Optimized: a hash map keyed by each string's sorted signature

blocks.text: This works because sorting a string always produces the exact same result for every anagram of it, regardless of the original order of its letters, so using that sorted form as the map key guarantees every string is appended to exactly the bucket shared by all of its true anagrams, and to no other.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["A string's sorted signature already exists as a map key","The string is appended directly to that existing bucket","It correctly joins every earlier anagram already grouped there"],["A string's sorted signature has never been seen before","A brand new map entry is created for it","A new group correctly begins for this distinct letter signature"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k log k), one sort per string.
Space: O(n times k), for the map holding every string.
10. Further Optimization: Counting Instead of Sorting

Sorting each string costs k log k. Since only lowercase English letters are involved, a character count signature (how many of each of the 26 letters appear) can be built in O(k) time instead, and used as the map key directly, entirely avoiding the sort.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result"],"rows":[["Count each letter: e:1, a:1, t:1, all others 0","signature: (0,1,0,...,0,1,...,1,...) as a 26 length count tuple"],["This exact same count signature is produced by \"tea\" and \"ate\"","they land in the same map bucket"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: a 26 letter count signature replaces sorting entirely

items: A 26 length count array is built for each string in a single linear pass, one increment per character, with no sorting involved at all.
That count array is converted into a hashable key, since raw arrays cannot be used directly as hash map keys in most languages.
Two strings produce the exact same count signature if and only if they contain exactly the same letters the same number of times, which is precisely the definition of being anagrams.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times k), building each count signature in linear time instead of sorting.
Space: O(n times k), unchanged.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Signature Type","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Brute force (scan every group)","O(n squared times k log k)","O(n times k)","Sorted, compared by manual scanning","Correct, but reintroduces a quadratic factor a hash map avoids."],["Optimized (hash map, sorted signature)","O(n times k log k)","O(n times k)","Sorted letters as the map key","A clean, standard O(n times k log k) solution."],["Further optimized (hash map, count signature)","O(n times k)","O(n times k)","Letter counts as the map key","The strongest answer, removing the sorting log factor entirely."]]}

blocks.text: The core idea across every version is finding a canonical signature that is identical for every anagram of a given string, then grouping directly by that signature with a hash map, whether the signature comes from sorting or from counting.

items: Scanning existing groups by hand instead of using a hash map, which reintroduces the quadratic factor the hash map is meant to remove.
Using a sorted string as the key when a much cheaper count based key would work just as well and avoid the log factor.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An array containing empty strings","All group together since they share the same, entirely empty, signature."],["Strings with repeated letters","The count based signature naturally distinguishes them correctly from strings with a different letter distribution."]]}

blocks.text: Mention the count based signature as a natural follow up optimization once the sorting based hash map solution is already working, since it directly addresses the log factor.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the log factor from sorting", think: a 26 letter count signature built in linear time, used as the hash map key instead.
If the interviewer says "what if the alphabet is not just lowercase letters", think: a hash map based count signature instead of a fixed size 26 array, the overall logic stays the same.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid scanning existing groups", think: a hash map keyed directly by the signature, removing the need to scan anything by hand.

items: Why does a sorted string, or a letter count, work equally well as a canonical signature for grouping anagrams?
How would the count based signature approach change if the alphabet were not limited to 26 lowercase letters?
How would you return just the number of groups, without materializing every group's full contents?
How would you group strings that are anagrams of each other after removing exactly one character from each?
How would you adapt this approach to group strings by whether they are anagrams of a specific fixed target string, rather than of each other?
Valid Anagram, whose exact same sorting and counting techniques for comparing two strings are extended here to group many strings at once using a hash map.
Find All Anagrams in a String, which reuses the same count signature idea, but applied to sliding windows of a longer string instead of a whole separate array of strings.
Any problem asking to bucket items by a shared property, where finding a canonical, hashable signature for that property turns grouping into a single hash map pass.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared times k log k) time, O(n times k) space. Optimized (sorted signature): O(n times k log k) time, O(n times k) space. Further optimized (count signature): O(n times k) time, O(n times k) space.

items: Pattern: a hash map keyed by a canonical letter signature, further optimized by replacing a sorted signature with a counted one.

Core Idea: any signature shared by every anagram of a string, sorted letters or letter counts, turns grouping into a direct hash map lookup, with a counted signature removing the sorting log factor entirely.
Time: O(n squared times k log k) for the brute force, O(n times k log k) for the sorted signature version, O(n times k) for the counted signature version.
Space: O(n times k) for all three approaches.
Most Important Observation: a canonical signature that is identical for every anagram of a string is what turns grouping from a comparison problem into a hash map lookup problem.
Interview Difficulty: the sorted signature version is standard and easy to derive; proactively offering the counted signature as a further refinement shows extra depth.
One line memory trick: group by a signature every anagram shares, sorted letters or, better, letter counts.
